segments.t: So it'll always bring it down, it'll always roll off, inflation will come back.
Well, what always happens is something else pops up and takes its place.
But if the economy keeps being resilient in the face of these shocks, for example, you
had these tariffs but you had no relative price decrease anywhere else, does that tell
you, and you're running above potential, does that automatically tell you policy's been
too accommodative?
Well, like I said, tariffs are kind of a special example because it's like if you
put on a 1% sales tax on everything in the economy, you'd say, yeah, okay, that's
a one-time thing.
Yeah.
With the oil shocks and the fact that there seems to be changes in the way oil shocks
have been persistent.
We had two oil shocks, not one.
We had one last spring.
We had one this fall.
It doesn't look like oil is going to be coming down dramatically anytime soon.
And then there's just this concern that people have started, what I was saying earlier,
people are starting to think 3% may be the norm.
And if you're a firm and the consumer's resilient and seems to be spending, why
not pass through three?
That's the kind of psychology I think we need to start breaking, is that it's not
going to be three and we have to do something to try to bring it back down.
We can't wait.
We can't do this in like the next two years.
I want to go back to this question of forward guidance.
It sounds to me like you're saying you wish the chair in this case or in other
cases would be using forward guidance to help policy here.
Well, the chair has his views and his way of wanting to communicate.
That's fine.
Those are his preferences.
I've been in this game a long time, and all the academic literature and
everything I know about central banking for 30 years is you want to use
communication as one of your tools.
That's my own view, and I'm going to stick with that view of we should be
using communication to do what we want to get the markets to help us do our job.
If you had to guess, how far does the Fed have to go now to get inflation
under control?
Well, I think first of all, you've got to take back the three insurance cuts we
put in last year.
So if the policy rate last summer in 2025 wasn't bringing inflation down,
getting back to that is...
